candidates.attacker_control: The template text itself (and any template fragment that reaches the engine: stored CMS/HubL content, user-supplied includes/imports/extends paths, or context values re-rendered by the nested-interpretation feature). No special context object is required: a literal such as a string or list already exposes Object.getClass().
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) Confirmed the property form 'x.class' is deliberately blocked (lines 16-18) and that no other code path filters method names, so this is the single guard being bypassed, not duplicate protection. (2) Confirmed readOnlyResolver=true by default only affects setValue in the read-only resolver composite (JinjavaConfig line 55; JinjavaInterpreterResolver lines 55-73), so it does not mitigate invoke(). (3) Confirmed Jinjava's own model expects method invocation to work: PyMap.items(), PyList.append(), FunctionLibrary/Functions docs and the ForTag 'my_dict.items()' example, plus the explicit METHOD_INVOCATIONS branch in ExtendedParser; this is why the blacklist exists at all. (4) Checked PrettyPrintFilter, which explicitly skips Class-typed properties and Object-declared read methods, showing the project elsewhere treats getClass as sensitive; JinjavaBeanELResolver does not. (5) Checked the JUEL dependency source is not in this snapshot, so the effective Feature set for Jinjava's builder could not be read directly.
candidates.impact: Sandbox escape: the only template-facing method/property restriction layer is bypassed, giving template authors reflective access to Class objects and arbitrary class loading/instantiation plus invocation of public methods on reachable instances. In typical JDK 8 deployments this is sufficient for remote code execution (scripting/reflection gadgets), and it also enables reading of classpath resources and calling application classes present in the render context. The intended protection (RESTRICTED_PROPERTIES 'class') is defeated by a one-name variation.
candidates.prerequisites: Render of an attacker-influenced template. JUEL's METHOD_INVOCATIONS feature must be active so that 'x.method()' parses (see uncertainty). The readOnlyResolver setting does not matter: it only affects setValue, while the escape uses invoke(). Full code execution additionally depends on classes available on the host classpath (e.g., scripting/reflection classes on JDK 8); without such a gadget the attacker still gets arbitrary class access/reflection.
candidates.root_cause: JinjavaBeanELResolver is the library's in-Java expression sandbox. RESTRICTED_PROPERTIES (lines 16-18) blocks the property name 'class', but RESTRICTED_METHODS (lines 20-26) only contains clone/hashCode/notify/notifyAll/wait. JinjavaBeanELResolver.invoke (lines 60-66) rejects a method only when its name is in RESTRICTED_METHODS, so the equivalent method form 'getClass' passes straight through to javax.el.BeanELResolver.invoke, which invokes Object.getClass() and returns a Class<?> object. Class objects then expose un-restricted public methods (forName, newInstance, getClassLoader, getResourceAsStream, etc.), so the property-level 'class' guard is trivially bypassed in method form.
candidates.title: EL sandbox escape: getClass() is not in JinjavaBeanELResolver's restricted-method list, exposing java.lang.Class to templates
candidates.trace: Expression containing 'X.getClass()' -> ExtendedParser.value() DOT branch sees LPAREN and builds an AstMethod when METHOD_INVOCATIONS is enabled (lines 316-325) -> AstMethod.eval calls ELContext.getELResolver().invoke(...) -> JinjavaInterpreterResolver.invoke (lines 82-97) first resolves the name as a property via getValue(...) (no 'getClass' bean property, so null) and then falls through to super.invoke -> Composite/BeanELResolver chain -> JinjavaBeanELResolver.invoke (lines 60-66): 'getClass' is not in RESTRICTED_METHODS, so super.invoke executes Object.getClass() and returns a Class<?> object. Chained invocations on that Class (forName/newInstance/getClassLoader) are likewise only checked against the same short blacklist and are not otherwise filtered, so the template can name and call arbitrary public methods of classes it loads or instantiates.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation was not performed (no code execution allowed). The exact JUEL feature set with which Jinjava constructs ExtendedSyntaxBuilder is not visible in this snapshot (Jinjava.java lines 79-90 set the builder class via the TreeBuilder property; the dependency source is out of scope), so 'x.method()' parsing is inferred from Jinjava's documented/exercised method-invocation behavior rather than proven. The severity of the final step depends on the host classpath/JDK; no end-to-end payload chain was verified. I also could not check upstream fix history, so I cannot state which release (if any) added 'getClass' to RESTRICTED_METHODS.
candidates.weakness_type: Sandbox escape / incomplete list of disallowed methods (CWE-184/CWE-693, leading to CWE-94 code injection and CWE-918-style reflective access)

coverage_summary: Scope: 223 repository files (benchmark module, build/docs, and 213 Java sources under src/main), NUL-scan and size filters applied; no src/test directory is present in this snapshot. I read the complete render/parse and expression-resolution path (Jinjava, JinjavaConfig, Context, JinjavaInterpreter, ExpressionResolver, JinjavaInterpreterResolver, JinjavaBeanELResolver, ExtendedParser/Scanner/Builder, tree + token classes, output nodes), the default library registries, all loader classes, all tag classes, and the large majority of the 60+ filters and 20+ exptests, plus util/date/random helpers; the remainder were skimmed for security-relevant logic. P1 index coverage is complete for syntax (213 parsed files, 0 parse errors, 1612 symbols, 2822 relations) but it is name/type/arity-based navigation only, with no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, or Spring runtime verification, and 2201 unresolved calls; absence of index records was not treated as evidence. Dependency sources (JUEL/de.odysseus.el, Guava, Jackson, jsoup, javassist) are outside the snapshot, so their runtime behavior was reasoned about but not verified.
limitations: No tests are included in the snapshot, so expected behavior and regression coverage could not be checked.

The JUEL (de.odysseus.el) dependency is not in scope; whether Feature.METHOD_INVOCATIONS is enabled for Jinjava's ExtendedSyntaxBuilder was inferred from Jinjava's own code/docs and cannot be proven from this snapshot.
P1 relations are syntactic candidates only (no control/data flow, 2201 unresolved calls, Spring annotations unverified), so reachability and exploitability of the candidate are not proven.
No code, scanners, or payloads were executed; all conclusions are static source review.

I could not consult upstream Jinjava history or advisories, so I cannot prove whether 'getClass' was ever restricted in a later version; the finding rests on the snapshot's internal security model (property 'class' blocked, dangerous Object methods blacklisted, getClass omitted).
Impact beyond the sandbox escape (full command execution) is host-dependent and not verified.

rejected_leads.lead: EscapeJsFilter does not escape single quote (') or forward slash (/): lines 83-95 only handle '"' and '\\', so output embedded in a single-quoted JavaScript string or in a <script> block could be broken out of (XSS).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible XSS gap and consistent with a possible reverted escaping fix, but the filter is an explicit opt-in helper, the 'safe embedding context' is application-defined, and I could not establish that upstream ever escaped those characters; treated as unconfirmed rather than submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlAttrFilter builds attributes with the map key inserted raw (`new StringBuilder(entry.getKey())`, lines 45-51; only values are XML-escaped by escapeXml10).
rejected_leads.reason: Attribute/script injection is possible only when dict keys are attacker-controlled (e.g., via fromjson); Jinja2 rejects such keys, Jinjava does not, but current Jinjava code appears to share this behavior, so it looks like a design gap rather than the introduced flaw.

rejected_leads.lead: FileLocator.resolveFileName returns absolute paths as-is and joins relative names without normalization (lines 44-52); README explicitly documents absolute-path includes as a known risk.
rejected_leads.reason: Documented intentional behavior of the non-default locator (default is ClasspathResourceLocator), not a hidden defect.

rejected_leads.lead: ImportTag pushes the unresolved helper string onto the import cycle stack (line 80) while loading the resolved path (line 91), unlike IncludeTag/ExtendsTag which push resolved paths.
rejected_leads.reason: Could weaken cycle detection if different raw strings resolve to the same template, but no concrete recursion/impact path was established; likely upstream behavior predating later fixes.

rejected_leads.lead: PrintTag renders the expression result without applying the context autoescape flag (lines 29-32), unlike ExpressionNode.render (lines 57-59).
rejected_leads.reason: Potential escaping bypass, but only inside {% autoescape %} blocks and only for the rarely used {% print %} form; impact weaker and arguably intended for old versions.

rejected_leads.lead: Nested interpretation is enabled by default (JinjavaConfig line 55 / Builder line 157) and ExpressionNode re-renders any value containing '{{' or '{%' (lines 46-55), which can amplify context-data driven template injection.
rejected_leads.reason: This is a documented, intentionally-defaulted configuration knob (CHANGES 2.2.3) rather than a concealed defect; it is an amplifier for the submitted candidate, not a separate root cause.

summary: Jinjava 2.4.6-SNAPSHOT template engine (223 files, ~213 Java sources; no tests in the snapshot). I reviewed the render/parse pipeline, EL resolution and the in-Java sandbox layer, tags (include/import/extends/from/macro/set/block/call), loaders, escape/output filters, and the function/exptest registries. The strongest distinct issue is in the template-expression sandbox: JinjavaBeanELResolver blocks the 'class' property and a short list of dangerous Object methods, but does not block the equivalent method name 'getClass', so a template expression can obtain a java.lang.Class object through the ordinary method-invocation path and then keep invoking public methods on it (reflection/class-loading surface). This is a sandbox escape with potential RCE, not merely a hardening gap. Other escape/validation gaps seen (escapejs single-quote/slash, xmlattr keys) are weaker or plausibly intentional and are listed only as rejected leads.
